Fathom: Autonomous Code-Level Optimization for Agentic Systems

Fathom is an upper-layer optimizer that profiles an agent, localizes expensive failure modes to source functions, patches code, and keeps changes only after repeated validation. The current evidence is a strong development-set accuracy gain on AgentFlow, not yet a held-out generalization result.

+6.6 pt Accuracy gain on dev120 train-split sample: 66.7% to 73.2%.
+0.4 calls/q The win costs about one extra LLM call per question, so it is not a free speedup.
3x gate Confirmation reports mean and standard deviation across repeated dev runs.

TL; DR

This quick validation does not yet prove that Fathom will improve Harvey directly, but it may offer useful positive and negative lessons for Harvey auto-optimization across design, logic, and implementation: how to turn rollout evidence into reversible harness edits, then filter those edits through measured quality and cost gates before they enter the OpenEvolve archive.

Pipeline overview

Fathom autonomous discovery pipeline

How to read it: the hand-drawn view summarizes the conservative loop: profile the target run, localize the highest-value code-level waste, patch one function, verify with repeated tests, then keep or revert.

  • Green path: accepted patches are kept with before/after metrics.
  • Red path: rejected candidates are cleanly reverted before the next attempt.
  • Audit output: each run leaves a patch decision, metrics, and journal trail.

Bottom line

What the current source supports

Credible dev-set win

The kept V3 code patch improves AgentFlow from 66.7% ± 0.8 to 73.2% ± 0.5 on a 120-question development sample drawn from the train split.

Real code leverage

The successful patch is not prompt wording. It changes python_coder.preprocess_code so AgentFlow can recover Python code from more model-output formats instead of failing and retrying.

Still not final proof

The held-out test split has not been run. The current claim should be framed as: Fathom found and validated a train-dev improvement that now needs external validation.

The strongest engineering point is not just the patch. It is the surrounding measurement discipline: cost/error diagnosis, function-level localization, compile and smoke checks, multi-run confirmation, runner-outage guards, and git-based rollback.

Repository map

Code structure

Fathom is split into an upper-layer optimizer and lower-layer target codebases. The optimizer lives in fathom/; target agents are expected under Agent-code/ as independent git submodules.

Area Role Key files
System adapter Defines editable code surface, trace parsing, evaluator, and cost field. fathom/evolve/target.py
Optimization loop Orchestrates profile, diagnose, patch, confirm, keep, and revert. fathom/evolve/loop.py
Diagnosis Turns traces into cost x error waste signatures and localizes likely functions. fathom/evolve/diagnose.py
Code patching Reads/replaces whole functions, checks compilation, and resolves git paths. fathom/evolve/codepatch.py
Validation Runs cheap screens and rigorous confirmations; applies noise and outage guards. fathom/evolve/fitness.py
Experiment artifacts Dev samples, scripts, the kept patch diff, and progress report. fathom/data/, fathom/scripts/, fathom/results/, fathom/reports/

Adapter boundary

The core design choice is a TargetSystem boundary. This keeps Fathom system-agnostic: adding a new agent should require an adapter, not changes to the optimizer brain.

Local checkout note

In the inspected checkout, Agent-code/agentflow is registered as a submodule but not initialized. The report therefore relies on Fathom source, scripts, reports, and stored patch artifacts; exact reruns require git submodule update --init --recursive.

Mechanism

Optimization flow and code analysis

1. System Flow

This HTML/CSS diagram mirrors the report's actual control path: profile, discover/localize, patch, verify, then keep or revert. The PNG above remains as the hand-drawn overview.

INPUT human goal + target system (code + how to run / score)
FATHOM LOOP autonomous, trace-grounded, git-reversible
1

PROFILE

Run the target agent and collect traces, accuracy, and LLM-call cost.

trace + metrics
2

DISCOVER + LOCALIZE

Cluster waste signatures and map the highest-value cluster to a source function.

file:func
3

PATCH

Rewrite that function, then compile-check and self-repair.

def ...
4

VERIFY

Run cheap screen, then 3x confirmation with a noise-aware objective gate.

mean +/- std

KEEP

  • git commit
  • keep patch
  • write audit journal

REVERT

  • git checkout
  • discard patch
  • continue to next cluster
Loop until no candidate improves beyond the validation gate.
OUTPUT kept patch or clean revert + before/after metrics + audit journal

2. Entry point

The autonomous workflow starts from fathom/scripts/fathom_auto.sh.

# --auto selects the autonomous discovery/localization/patch path.
python3 -m evolve.loop --iters 2 --auto \
  --skip-targets "models/executor.py:extract_explanation_and_command" \
  --advice "Keep the EXACT function name/signature/decorators..." \
  --baseline-json .openfable/baseline_patch1.json \
  --workdir .openfable/fathom_auto

The --auto flag routes execution to run_autonomous(). The --skip-targets argument excludes already-evaluated functions so the localizer must search for a new plausible root cause.

3. run_autonomous(): orchestrator

Core location: fathom/evolve/loop.py#L302.

This is the spine of V3.1: screen once, discover waste clusters, build an editable function menu, localize the best cluster, then send the target to the patch gate.

# One current run produces trace evidence for discovery.
cur_out = f"{args.workdir}/auto_cur.json"
fitness.screen(cur_out)
disc = diagnose.discover_waste(cur_out, top=8)

# The function menu is built from adapter-exposed source files.
idx = codepatch.code_index()

for c in disc["clusters"]:
    loc = diagnose.localize_target(c, idx, exclude=skip | tried)
    target = {"file": loc["file"], "func": loc["func"]}
    kept, cand = _patch_gate(target, desc, examples, advice, ...)

This function does not hard-code AgentFlow internals. It relies on the target adapter for trace parsing and on code_index() for discovering editable functions.

4. discover_waste(): trace-driven waste discovery

Core location: fathom/evolve/diagnose.py#L239.

The discovery step converts raw AgentFlow traces into ranked waste clusters. The key score stays deliberately simple: prioritize failures that are both expensive and wrong-correlated.

# Adapter supplies normalized error signatures and trigger examples.
sigs = {_norm_err(s) for s in ts.error_sigs(r) if _norm_err(s)}
examples = ts.command_examples(r)

# cost share x wrong rate = target priority
cs = calls / total
er = wrong / q
waste_score = round(cs * er * 100, 1)

waste_score = call_share * wrong_rate. The loop prioritizes failure clusters that are both expensive in LLM calls and correlated with wrong answers.

5. Target adapter: AgentFlow trace parsing

Core location: fathom/evolve/target.py.

The adapter boundary is why the core can stay system-agnostic. For AgentFlow, tool failures come from tool_result_N, and malformed model commands come from tool_commander_N_response.

# Error signatures are the trace symptoms Fathom can cluster.
def _af_error_sigs(row):
    tr = row.get("trace", {})
    sigs = []
    for k, v in tr.items():
        if k.startswith("tool_result") and "error" in str(v).lower():
            sigs.append(str(v))
    return sigs

# Command examples are concrete failing inputs for the patch proposer.
def _af_command_examples(row):
    tr = row.get("trace", {})
    return [
        str(v) for k, v in tr.items()
        if k.startswith("tool_commander") and k.endswith("response")
    ]

This is the target-specific part. Everything above this boundary can remain reusable for another agent as long as that agent exposes equivalent trace, code, and evaluator hooks.

6. code_index(): building the function menu

Core location: fathom/evolve/codepatch.py#L65.

code_index() scans editable source files and creates the menu the localizer can choose from. This removes the need for a hand-written target registry in autonomous mode.

# Each menu item gives the localizer just enough source context.
{
    "file": rel,
    "func": function_name,
    "sig": function_signature,
    "head": first_non_comment_body_line
}

The important detail is that the localizer receives a bounded menu of editable functions, not the entire repository. That keeps localization tractable and makes the result patchable.

7. localize_target(): mapping waste to source

Core location: fathom/evolve/diagnose.py#L332.

The localizer receives the waste signature, stats, trigger examples, grep hits, editable function menu, and excluded already-tried targets. It returns strict JSON so the rest of the loop can stay deterministic.

# The LLM chooses one concrete function, but the choice is grounded in grep + traces.
{
  "file": "...",
  "func": "...",
  "why": "...",
  "fix_hint": "...",
  "confident": true
}

The design choice is grep-grounded localization: if the source literally raises, emits, or parses the observed failure text, that evidence anchors the model's function choice.

8. Patch gate

Core location: fathom/evolve/loop.py#L216.

Once localization picks a target function, the patch gate owns the lifecycle: propose, compile, self-repair, screen, confirm, keep or revert.

# Candidate generation can be single-shot or best-of-N.
code = _propose_compiling(target, current_code, desc, examples, advice, gfile, codepatch)

# Cheap screen drops catastrophic candidates before full confirmation.
s = fitness.screen(f"{args.workdir}/{tag}_rank{j}.json", n=args.rank_n)
catastrophic = s["acc"] < 0.6 * best["acc_mean"] or s["calls"] < 1.5

# The final decision uses rigorous confirmation, then reverts by git unless kept.
cand = fitness.confirm(f"{args.workdir}/{tag}_confirm_c{c['j']}")
_git("checkout", gfile)
keep, reason = _gate(cand)

The gate is deliberately skeptical. A candidate must compile, survive a cheap screen, and then pass repeated confirmation before it can be kept.

9. Evaluation integrity

Core location: fathom/evolve/fitness.py.

The validation layer is the main guard against false positives. It rejects noisy wins, broken patches that look cheap because they crash early, and runner-outage survivorship bias.

# Confirm measures repeated runs and records mean/std for accuracy and cost.
def confirm(out_dir: str, runs: int = 3, data: str = "data/dev120_train.jsonl",
            n: int = 120, workers: int = 48, min_complete: float = 0.8) -> dict:
    for r in range(runs):
        run = _run_dev(data, n, workers, f"{out_dir}/run{r+1}.json")
        completed = sum(1 for row in run["rows"] if "error" not in row)
        if completed < min_complete * n:
            continue

# If too few runs are healthy, the loop raises and reverts instead of reporting a win.
if healthy < 2:
    raise RuntimeError("confirm untrustworthy")

screen() is for fast rejection; confirm() is for evidence. The final report should use the latter, because it reports mean and standard deviation across repeated runs.

Kept code-level patch

fathom/results/patch1_preprocess_code.diff

The kept patch fixes the brittle Python-code extractor by accepting common model-output shapes instead of raising immediately.

# Ordered fallbacks: tagged fence, generic fence, unclosed fence, bare code.
def preprocess_code(code):
    import re
    if not code:
        return ""
    code = str(code)
    for p in [
        r"```(?:python|py|python3)\s*(.*?)\s*```",
        r"```\s*(.*?)\s*```",
        r"```(?:python|py|python3)\s*(.*)",
        r"```\s*(.*)"
    ]:
        m = re.search(p, code, re.DOTALL | re.IGNORECASE)
        if m:
            return m.group(1).strip()

    # Final useful fallback: recover Python-looking code from prose.
    m = re.search(r"(?m)^\s*(?:def |import |from |class |print\(|[a-zA-Z0-9_]+\s*=).*", code, re.DOTALL)
    if m:
        return m.group(0).strip()
    return code.strip()
Evaluation design

Experiment setup

Target agent AgentFlow, expected under Agent-code/agentflow as a submodule pinned to lupantech/AgentFlow.
Runner model Qwen-2.5-7B via OpenRouter, matching the AgentFlow runner setup in the repository scripts.
Optimizer model Gemini-3.1-pro-preview proposes patches. It does not answer benchmark questions.
Data dev90_train.jsonl, dev120_train.jsonl, and dev300_train.jsonl, sampled from GSM8K-train and MATH-train. The reported headline uses dev120 and 3 repeated runs.
Metrics Accuracy, hard-problem accuracy, LLM calls per question, and optional wall time from the target adapter.
Keep gate Compile check, smoke screen, 3x confirm, noise-band gate, instability guard, hard accuracy floor, and git rollback on reject.
Integrity boundary The reported numbers are from a development set sampled from train. The held-out test set is explicitly not run yet.

Why this avoids trivial leakage

The optimizer patches code, while the runner answers benchmark questions. The optimizer model is not used as the benchmark solver, which reduces direct answer-injection risk.

Remaining contamination risk

Because the development data comes from train splits, any final claim must be confirmed on held-out test data and preferably on a second agent.

Interpretation

The patch improves correctness, especially on hard problems, by reducing a brittle tool-extraction failure mode. It does not reduce cost in the headline result; it trades a small calls increase for a larger accuracy gain.

V3.1 reportedly reproduced the win fully autonomously. V3.2's clean confirmation remains blocked by transient runner/API instability and should be rerun.

What worked

Good lessons

1. Code-level fixes matter

The winning intervention was inside a tool parser, not a prompt. This validates the premise that agent failures can live in glue code, parsing, and control logic.

2. Cost x error is a useful targeting rule

Ranking failures by both expense and wrongness focuses patch attempts on bugs that are likely to matter for both performance and correctness.

3. Git rollback is the right safety primitive

Function-level edits are risky. A clean git checkout after rejected screens or confirms keeps experiments reversible and prevents hidden state accumulation.

4. Multi-run gates caught false positives

The confirmation gate and outage guard caught noise artifacts, broken patches, and survivorship-bias results before they were reported as wins.

What did not work

Bad lessons

1. The headline is not a speedup

The project motivation includes cheaper agent execution, but the current best result increases calls per question from 9.77 to 10.2.

2. The evidence is still train-dev only

A held-out test run is mandatory before claiming generalization. Current numbers should remain framed as development evidence.

3. Generality is designed, not proven

The adapter boundary is clean, but only one target agent and one runner have produced the reported win. A second agent is needed.

4. Best-of-N needs stable infrastructure

V3.2 is conceptually useful, but transient runner/API crashes blocked clean confirmation. This makes infra health a first-class requirement, not an afterthought.

Action plan

Next steps

  1. Initialize and pin the target submodule. Run git submodule update --init --recursive, record the AgentFlow commit, and ensure the local checkout matches the reported patch target.
  2. Run held-out test evaluation. Evaluate baseline and kept patch on a held-out test split with the same runner, same seeds if applicable, and the same 3x confirmation logic.
  3. Add instrumentation for latency and cost. Track LLM calls, wall time, tool calls, token counts, and dollar cost per question so speed/cost claims are measured rather than inferred.
  4. Rerun V3.2 under stable runner conditions. Keep the best-of-N design, but separate infrastructure failures from candidate quality.
  5. Port the adapter to a second agent. This is the cleanest test of whether Fathom is a reusable optimizer or a strong AgentFlow case study.
  6. Run ablations. Compare hand-seeded V3, autonomous V3.1, best-of-N V3.2, no self-repair, no outage guard, and no cost x error ranking.

Recommended claim wording

"Fathom found and validated a code-level development-set improvement in AgentFlow, raising accuracy by 6.6 points at a small cost increase. The result is promising but should not be treated as final until held-out and second-agent validation are complete."

Harvey validation

Where this quick validation could help Harvey auto-optimization

This Fathom experiment is best read as a quick validation of the mechanics that Harvey auto-optimization may need: read execution evidence, identify a concrete harness weakness, propose a reversible edit, and keep it only after measured validation. It is not yet proof that the same loop improves Harvey, but it suggests several places where the approach could transfer into the Harvey/OpenEvolve design.

Reference

Agentic AlphaEvolve for the Harvey Harness design doc

1. Turning rollouts into edit targets

The prototype shows one way to convert traces into ranked failure targets. For Harvey, the analogous path is to dump standard-eval rollouts, inspect them for recurring legal workflow failures, and point the mutator at the skill, tool, or scaffold most likely to help.

2. Making automated edits safer

Reversible patches, compile checks, multi-run gates, outage guards, and audit journals are directly useful for Harvey harness evolution. They give the mutator freedom to try code-level changes while keeping failed candidates contained and easy to reject.

3. Measuring quality-cost tradeoffs

The AgentFlow result improved accuracy but raised calls per question, which is a useful warning. Harvey auto-optimization should track canonical score, latency, LLM calls, tool calls, token cost, dollar cost, and held-out performance from the start.

4. Testing the adapter boundary

Fathom's target adapter is a small proof point for separating the optimizer from the system being optimized. Porting that boundary to Harvey would clarify what the mutator needs from the harness: editable files, rollout schema, eval command, and cost fields.
